desc:
An AI cost and ROI review before you commit shows what a project will cost and what it could save. Ecom Swift LLC works out setup cost, running cost, staff time and likely savings for one idea, so you decide with evidence instead of a sales pitch.

## What is an AI cost and ROI review?

An AI cost and ROI review is a short written estimate of what an AI tool or project would cost to start and run, set against the time or money it could save. It shows low, likely and high figures and states every assumption behind them. The point is to make the decision before you pay, not after.

ROI means return on investment. For a small business that usually comes down to a simple question: will this pay for itself, and how long will that take?

## Why the numbers matter before you buy

Most AI tools are sold on a monthly price and a promise. The price on the pricing page is rarely the whole cost. Someone has to set the tool up, connect it to your systems, write the instructions, check the output and fix mistakes. That time belongs on the bill, even if no invoice arrives for it.

Without a review, two things tend to go wrong. You either skip a good idea because it sounds expensive, or you buy a tool that costs more in staff attention than it ever saves. A clear estimate protects you from both mistakes.

## How a cost review improves your results

The review improves decisions, and decisions drive results. When you can see the payback period, you can compare an AI idea against other uses of the same budget, such as hiring help, buying stock or running ads. When you can see the worst case, you know what you stand to lose if the idea underperforms.

Estimates work because they force the hidden parts into the open. How many hours a week does this task take today? Who does it? What does an error cost? Once those answers are written down, the saving is no longer a feeling. It is a range you can test and challenge. Real outcomes still depend on how well the tool is used, so we present ranges and never a single promised figure.

## What a good cost and ROI estimate includes

- One clearly described idea or tool, with the task it would change.
- Setup cost: licences, build time, connecting accounts, and any outside help.
- Monthly running cost: subscriptions, usage charges and extra seats.
- Staff time to manage the tool, review its work and handle exceptions.
- The time or money saved today, based on how the task is really done.
- A low, likely and high view of the savings.
- The payback period, shown in plain months.
- Assumptions listed in full, so you can change any of them.
- Risk notes covering data, quality and dependence on one vendor.
- A short recommendation: go ahead, adjust, wait or skip.

## How we run the review

We start with a short conversation about the idea you are weighing and the task behind it. We ask how the work is done now, who does it, how often and how long it takes. Then we price the options using the plan details you share and the public information vendors publish.

From there we build the estimate. In the Basic package you receive a report for one idea. The Standard package compares two ideas or tools side by side and adds staff management time and a payback view. The Premium package models several options in an editable spreadsheet, so you can change an assumption and watch the result move, and it ends with a results call. Add-ons cover an extra idea, a one page summary for a board or partner, and a list of questions to put to vendors.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Bring real task details, even rough ones, such as hours spent and who does the work.
- Include the cost of your own time and your staff's time.
- Ask for the worst case as well as the likely case.
- Compare more than one option before choosing.
- Revisit the estimate after a few months of real use.

**Avoid:**
- Trusting a vendor's own savings claims without checking them against your tasks.
- Counting the best-case saving as the expected saving.
- Ignoring training, checking and clean-up time.
- Signing a long contract before the numbers are clear.
- Treating the estimate as fixed once your business changes.

## Who this is for

Owners of small shops and service firms often ask this question before spending on a subscription. A store owner might be weighing a tool that writes product descriptions. A clinic manager might be considering a tool that drafts patient reminders. A founder preparing a funding or partner conversation might need a tidy page showing the numbers behind a plan.

It also suits anyone who has received a quote from a builder and wants a second view of whether the figures make sense.

## What we need from you

Send a short description of the idea, the task it would affect, and roughly how the task is done today. If you have a vendor quote or a pricing page, send that too. We never ask for passwords. If we need to see how a task works in one of your tools, you can add us as a staff or team user with limited access, or simply share screenshots instead.

After you order we reply with a short checklist, ask any follow-up questions, and deliver the written estimate in the format your package includes.
